issues.legal_issue: A law governing the withholding of property from its rightful owner must limit the taking to a public purpose.
material_facts: The property had been wrongly treated as evacuee property, and the rightful owner was entitled to its restoration.
The challenged law allowed the government to withhold restoration if it considered restoration inexpedient or impracticable, including for reasons beyond the occupation of a displaced person.
Instead of restoring the property, the government could provide other property or cash, while its discretion was not confined to a public purpose.
issues.conclusion: The law violated the public-purpose requirement because it allowed property to be withheld for reasons serving government convenience or the convenience of a private occupant rather than a public purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2) of the Constitution required an acquisition or requisition to be for a public purpose. Although rehabilitation of displaced persons was a public purpose, that objective did not justify a power to withhold restoration for non-public reasons. The Court referred to Amar Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property, Punjab, [1957] SCR 801, for the statutory background; it did not rely on that case as the basis for this constitutional holding.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_tak: A party in a constitutional challenge disputes a law that permits property to be taken or withheld from its rightful owner.
predicates.law_allows_withholding_for_nonpublic_rea: The law permits the government to withhold restoration for reasons that can serve government or private convenience rather than a public purpose.

issues.definition: When a property-taking law is challenged and permits withholding property for non-public reasons, the law fails the public-purpose requirement.

issues.legal_issue: A law authorizing the taking of property must fix compensation or prescribe adequate principles for determining it.
material_facts: The law permitted substitute property to be provided, but did not specify when the property's value was to be assessed.
The law also permitted cash to be paid without requiring that it equal the value of the property withheld or prescribing a standard for the amount.
The owner's title to the original property was extinguished after substitute property or cash was provided.
issues.conclusion: The law violated the compensation requirement because it neither fixed compensation nor prescribed adequate principles for determining it.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2) of the Constitution required a law authorizing acquisition or requisition to fix compensation or specify the principles on which, and the manner in which, compensation was to be determined or given. A direction to provide property of nearly the same value was inadequate without specifying when value was to be assessed; the cash alternative supplied no adequate standard. The Court referred to Amar Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property, Punjab, [1957] SCR 801, for statutory background, not as the basis for this holding.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_tak: A party in a constitutional challenge disputes a law that permits property to be taken or withheld from its rightful owner.
predicates.law_lacks_adequate_compensation_standard: The law provides neither a fixed compensation amount nor adequate principles for determining compensation, including a standard for assessing value or the cash amount.

issues.definition: When a property-taking law is challenged and lacks an adequate compensation standard, the law fails the compensation requirement.

issues.legal_issue: A property-transfer scheme that cannot be separated into valid and invalid applications is invalid as a whole when its operation includes acquisitions requiring constitutional property-taking safeguards.
material_facts: The law applied where the rightful owner's title could be extinguished after substitute property or cash was provided.
The Court observed that, where the property remained in the compensation pool, extinguishing the owner's title would vest the property in the government.
The Court acknowledged that a case in which title had vested in a displaced person might fall under a different constitutional provision, but held that the law was not severable.
issues.conclusion: The law was not severable and had to be declared invalid as a whole.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered Article 31(2A) of the Constitution, under which some transfers of title to a displaced person might be treated differently, but held that the challenged section was not severable. The Court therefore declared the section void as a whole under Article 31(2).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_integrated_p: A party in a constitutional challenge disputes a single scheme for transferring property and extinguishing the former owner's title.
predicates.scheme_covers_government_and_private_ves: The scheme operates in circumstances where title may vest in the government and in circumstances where title may vest in a private recipient.
predicates.scheme_is_not_severable: The scheme's valid and invalid applications cannot be separated from one another.

issues.definition: A challenged property-transfer scheme is invalid as a whole when it covers both government and private vesting contexts and cannot be severed.

issues.legal_issue: A new challenge to an administrative order that was not raised before the High Court will not be considered for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: During the appeal, counsel challenged the validity of the order releasing the property to its rightful owner on the ground that the occupants had not been heard.
That challenge had not been raised in the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to allow the challenge to be raised at that stage.
issues.legal_principle: The Court would not entertain at the appellate stage a challenge that had not been raised before the High Court.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is before the Supreme Court in an appeal from a High Court decision.
predicates.challenge_not_raised_before_high_court: A party advances a challenge in the Supreme Court that was not raised before the High Court.

issues.definition: In a Supreme Court appeal, a challenge not raised before the High Court is not entertained for the first time.
